One-sentence judgment: camera and photographic equipment repairers are not about "swapping parts"; they use precision gauges and hand tools to disassemble equipment to drawings and technical specifications, diagnose faults, adjust and align optical and mechanical mechanisms, test shutter and metering accuracy, and deliver reviewable repair and test records. O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), does not mark it Bright Outlook, and gives an interest code of RC. The core boundary: you may disassemble, adjust, test, and record within the authorized scope, but you may not work before energy has been isolated, may not change the safety-related settings of a customer's equipment on your own, and may not treat "being able to fix it" as proof that precision verification and records can be skipped.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to disassemble step by step and record the condition and part positions before taking it apart; you can accept long periods of sitting, using eyes and feel together, and work with high precision requirements; you are willing to check shutter, metering, and focus with precision gauges and test instruments rather than calling it done by feel; with old models that change often and have hard-to-find spares, you are willing to consult drawings, trial-produce parts, and keep records; and you accept a daily routine centered on repair records and test data.

Conditions for pausing major investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop from reading drawings, disassembly, diagnosis, adjustment, and precision testing through delivery records; or you are unwilling to do power-down and discharge per standards and unwilling to keep test records, wanting only to "open it up and look"; also, do not treat being able to shoot and repair your own home camera as proof that you can independently take on commercial and motion picture camera repair.

Education, credentials, and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0); it usually requires vocational school training, related on-the-job experience, or an associate degree, plus one to two years of on-the-job training (including apprenticeship forms). In the United States, job requirements are set by employers and there is usually no uniform practice license; the O*NET certification page can be used to discover candidate credentials but does not equal a license, an employer appointment, or signing authority. In mainland China, the Occupational Classification Code of the People's Republic of China (2022 edition) has no one-to-one sub-category matching this entry, and the related duties may fall under optoelectronic instrument, audiovisual equipment, and precision instrument repair positions, so they must be judged by the actual duties of the position, and it is made clear that the Chinese page language does not constitute a China-equivalent occupation or wage mapping. Disassembly and testing authorization, precision determination authority, and the authority to quote externally and confirm delivery are different things and cannot substitute for one another.

In one sentence: this is a role that turns "does the equipment still work, and does it measure accurately" into reviewable evidence; the outputs are repair and adjustment completed to standards, precision and function test data, spare part replacement and modification records, and traceable delivery notes; it is not the approving role for equipment design and safety certification, nor does it replace the applicable jurisdiction's requirements for electrical safety and product compliance. The work of this occupation falls into three categories: first, disassembly, reassembly, and adjustment (using hand tools to disassemble equipment to reach faults, and adjusting camera and photographic mechanisms plus rangefinders, viewfinders, shutters, light meters, and lens systems, and cleaning, lubricating, and polishing lenses); second, testing and calibration (using precision gauges to test performance, focus, aperture, mounts, and film transport mechanisms, using timing instruments to calibrate light meters, shutters, and lens-barrel mounts, and measuring parts to verify specified dimensions or settings); third, diagnosis and delivery (diagnosing faults by combining the equipment with developed film and laboratory reports, reading drawings and specifications to determine repair and manufacturing methods, making or modifying parts per specifications, recording test data and processes, proposing design change suggestions, and delivering notes). All three share the same chain built around disassembly records, precision verification, and reviewable test data.
Disassembly, reassembly, and adjustment

Editorial process example: check the model, method, fault, and safety conditions, then have personnel with the actual competence and scope diagnose, disassemble, reassemble, and adjust, verify, and record per the method; a reader cannot repair equipment just by following the steps. Electrical risk is checked against the actual model, components, and energy; stopping or unplugging does not necessarily eliminate stored energy. In the U.S., OSHA1910.333 generally requires exposed electrical parts to be de-energized first, and lockout/tagout for fixed equipment with qualified verification and restoration has additional conditions; this text grants no authority to discharge, open equipment live, or restart, and the specific safety procedures are implemented by competent personnel under the applicable rules.
Testing and calibration

Use precision gauges to test performance, focus, aperture, and mounts → use timing instruments to calibrate metering and shutters → measure parts to verify dimensional settings → compare item by item against specification values → record deviations and disposition → produce test and calibration records.

Editorial handover suggestion: check retesting, parts, records, limitations, and exception handling; equipment restoration conditions must be confirmed under the actual safety procedures, and no real employer process was obtained.

Camera and photographic equipment repairers have as their core output repair and adjustment results, precision and function test data, and traceable delivery records; aerospace engineering and operations technologists provide engineering support and operations data work in the aviation field; electrical and electronic engineering technologists build, test, and repair electrical and electronic systems under the direction of engineers; electromechanical technicians install, commission, and repair electromechanical equipment and automation systems; calibration technologists and technicians perform calibration and traceability of measurement devices within a metrology system; photonics technicians handle the processing, assembly, and testing of optical and photonic devices. Similar names or being in the same equipment and electronics chain do not mean that disassembly and reassembly authorization, precision determination authority, and external delivery confirmation authority are interchangeable.
Core purpose

Restore equipment to a usable state with trustworthy measurements: ensure mechanical and optical fit through drawing-based disassembly, reassembly, and adjustment, ensure precision through precision gauges and timing instruments, and make results reviewable through test records.
Main objects and basis

The objects are cameras and photographic and video equipment (including commercial video and motion picture cameras, aerial cameras, and drone cameras), optical and mechanical mechanisms (lens systems, shutters, apertures, light meters, viewfinders, film transport mechanisms), electronic and electrical components, engineering drawings and specifications, precision gauges and timing instruments, and spare parts and modification materials; the basis is engineering drawings and technical specifications, manufacturer service manuals and tolerance requirements, precision and function test criteria, spare part and material substitution rules, the power-down, discharge, and energy isolation requirements of electrical safety, and the company's inspection and delivery procedures.
Core process

Reading drawings and confirming the fault, power-down and energy isolation, disassembly and condition records, diagnosis and determining the plan, adjustment and replacement and modification, cleaning, lubricating, and polishing, precision gauge and timing instrument testing and calibration, recording test data and processes, reassembly and retesting, and delivery with notes.
Main outputs

Repair and adjustment results completed to standards, precision and function test data, shutter and metering calibration records, part measurement and dimensional setting verification records, specification notes for replaced and modified parts, repair reports and test data records, and delivery and usage limitation notes.
Accountable party

Editorial responsibility interface: repair, testing, design, certification, and safety management may be separated or combined; check against the real system, and the occupation name does not automatically assign exclusive authority.
Authority and approval

Article 28 of China's Work Safety Law requires passing training before taking up the post with records kept; Article 30 requires checking special operations against the actual catalog and tasks separately, and this does not imply that all camera repair is special operations; the rights under Articles 54—55 to refuse violations and to stop and evacuate for direct danger are not replaced by internal authorization. Individual permits, manufacturer partnerships, models, equipment, and signing scope were not comprehensively checked this round, so it cannot be stated generally that no license is required.

Repair and test records must be interpreted according to the actual method and conditions and do not automatically equal design or safety certification; this round did not comprehensively check product standards and certification rules, so no compliance conclusion can be signed based on this page.

Before starting, check at least six items: job duties (camera optical mechanisms, electronic components, or equipment modification and assembly), the range of models that may be disassembled and the tool authorization scope, the signing and review process for precision test and calibration data, electrical safety and energy isolation requirements, spare part sources and substitution rules, and whether you are responsible for customer communication and quoting.

Camera and photographic equipment repairers (O*NET-SOC 49-9061.00) repair and adjust cameras and photographic equipment, including commercial video and motion picture camera equipment. Daily work includes: using hand tools to adjust camera and photographic mechanisms as well as rangefinders and viewfinders, shutters, light meters, and lens systems; disassembling equipment to reach faulty areas; using precision gauges to test equipment performance, lens system focus, aperture alignment, lens mounts, or film transport mechanisms; cleaning and lubricating cameras and polishing lenses; purchasing parts or materials; using timing instruments to calibrate and verify light meters, shutter and aperture action, and lens-barrel mounts; diagnosing faults by combining the equipment with developed film or laboratory reports; reading and understanding engineering drawings, diagrams, instructions, or specifications to determine the needed repairs, manufacturing methods, and operations; measuring parts to verify specified dimensions or settings (such as shutter speed or metering accuracy); making or modifying defective electronic, electrical, or mechanical parts per specifications using lathes, milling machines, planers, grinders, or precision hand tools; installing electrical components and wiring and loading cassettes or film in aerial camera housings to drawings and with hand tools and soldering equipment; assembling aerial cameras, still or motion picture cameras, photographic equipment, or mounts to drawings and with bench machines; recording test data and manufacturing processes on reports; laying out reference points and dimensions on parts to be machined or on metal stock; proposing design changes or upgrades for microphotography, processing, or photographic equipment; and repairing and calibrating drone cameras and equipment used for aerial photography and videography. It carries responsibility for disassembly, reassembly, and adjustment, precision verification, test records, and delivery notes, but does not replace equipment design and certification approval, nor the applicable jurisdiction's electrical safety and product compliance responsibility.

paragraphs: This page compares camera and photographic equipment repairers with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is better suited to. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupation descriptions and do not mean the job titles are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career direction and core outputs are based on O*NET 49-9061.00 and the official descriptions of the adjacent entries (U.S. scope); disassembly and testing authorization, precision determination authority, and external delivery confirmation authority must be verified separately for each company and jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut for changing careers.

The table below compares the differences in duties and outputs between camera and photographic equipment repairers and the adjacent directions; the basis for judging is the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required authorization, not how similar the job titles are.

Technicians in that direction support engineering and operations in specific industry settings and are bound by industry standards; this occupation focuses on the repair and adjustment of cameras and photographic and video equipment, and is accountable for equipment status and precision.

If you would rather do engineering support and operations in an aviation setting, look first at the aerospace engineering and operations technologist direction; if you would rather do equipment repair and precision testing, look first at this occupation.
Provide engineering support, data compilation, and operations coordination in the aviation field, with output mainly engineering data and operations records.
Aerospace Engineering and Operations Technologists and Technicians

Electrical and electronic engineering technologists lean toward system build-up and electrical and electronic fault repair, with criteria coming from system function; this occupation leans toward the adjustment and precision verification of optical and mechanical mechanisms, with criteria coming from optical and mechanical tolerances.

If you would rather build and repair electrical and electronic systems, look first at the electrical and electronic engineering technologist direction; if you would rather repair optical and mechanical mechanisms, look first at this occupation.
Build, test, and repair electrical and electronic systems under the direction of engineers, with output mainly test data and repair records.
Electrical and Electronic Engineering Technologists and Technicians

Electromechanical technicians deal with electromechanical systems and automation control, and their responsibility lies in equipment operation and interlocked functions; this occupation deals with precision optical and mechanical mechanisms, and its responsibility lies in adjustment precision and test data.

If you would rather commission and repair electromechanical equipment and automation systems, look first at the electromechanical technician direction; if you would rather do hand adjustment and testing of precision equipment, look first at this occupation.
Install, commission, and repair electromechanical equipment and automation systems, with output mainly equipment operating status and commissioning records.
Electro-Mechanical Technicians

Calibration technologists and technicians handle measurement standards and uncertainty per metrology procedures, and their responsibility lies in whether the measurement is trustworthy; this occupation restores equipment function per manufacturer drawings and specifications, and its responsibility lies in whether the equipment is restored to a usable state and its precision.

If you would rather work on reference standards and value traceability, look first at the calibration technologist and technician direction; if you would rather do equipment repair and mechanism adjustment, look first at this occupation.
Perform calibration and traceability of measurement devices within a metrology system, with output mainly calibration records and deviation notes.
Calibration Technologists and Technicians

Photonics technicians work on the manufacturing and optoelectronic performance testing of optical devices, usually in a production or laboratory environment; this occupation works on fault diagnosis and repair of finished equipment, dealing with the disassembly, reassembly, and adjustment of already-assembled units.

If you would rather do the processing and performance testing of optical devices, look first at the photonics technician direction; if you would rather do repair and adjustment of complete units, look first at this occupation.
Process, assemble, and test optical and photonic devices, with output mainly device performance data and assembly records.
Photonics Technicians

Audiovisual equipment installers and repairers focus on system installation, wiring, commissioning, and on-site troubleshooting, with system-level audiovisual equipment as the object; this occupation focuses on mechanism adjustment and precision testing of single precision photographic and video units, with work leaning more toward fine operations.

If you would rather do audiovisual system installation and on-site troubleshooting, look first at the audiovisual equipment installer and repairer direction; if you would rather do mechanism repair of precision equipment, look first at this occupation.
Install and repair audiovisual equipment and systems, with output mainly system availability and on-site installation records.
Audiovisual Equipment Installers and Repairers

Conclusion: the choice of direction is based on the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required authorization, not on how similar the names are; once the direction is set, check the target position item by item for the models that may be disassembled and the tool authorization, the signing process for precision test and calibration data, electrical safety and energy isolation requirements, and shifts and spare part conditions, and keep written confirmation.

entries.answer: The main risks are electric shock and secondary equipment damage from live work or unisolated energy, equipment that cannot be restored due to a wrong disassembly sequence or lost parts, rework and loss of trust from delivering without precision testing, occupational health risk from contaminant and chemical contact, and compliance risk from modifying parts or making external promises beyond authorization; control depends on power-down and discharge and energy isolation, disassembling in manual sequence with records, testing with precision gauges and timing instruments and keeping records, ventilation and personal protection, and clear authorization and escalation procedures.

entries.answer: Fit signals are being able to read drawings and specifications and disassemble in sequence, keeping parts and records orderly, completing one reviewable precision test with precision gauges and timing instruments, and stopping and asking first when energy is not isolated or the model is unfamiliar; being able to shoot and repair a home camera is not enough to prove competence — what matters is whether there are reviewable repair records, precision test data, and safe working habits.

subject.name: Camera and Photographic Equipment Repairers
subject.summary: This page's entry corresponds to camera and photographic equipment repairers (O*NET-SOC 49-9061.00): repairing and adjusting cameras and photographic equipment, including commercial video and motion picture camera equipment — disassembling and diagnosing to drawings and specifications, adjusting optical and mechanical mechanisms, cleaning, lubricating, and polishing lenses, testing and calibrating with precision gauges and timing instruments, and making or modifying parts with records kept; the work is mainly fine disassembly and testing while sitting for long periods under environmentally controlled indoor conditions (91% work indoors in an environmentally controlled place every day, 78% continuous hand use, 46% continuous sitting), and its responsibility does not equal equipment design and safety certification approval, nor does it replace the applicable jurisdiction's electrical safety and product compliance responsibility.
